chief_complaint: greasy, yellowish scales and redness on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest
hpi_details: 45M with Parkinson disease presenting with chronic pruritic erythematous plaques covered by greasy yellow scales on nasolabial folds and dandruff responding to 2% Ketoconazole shampoo and low-potency hydrocortisone cream.
ideas: He thinks the flaking and redness are just stubborn dandruff and unwashed skin because his hand tremors make it hard to scrub his face and scalp thoroughly.
concerns: He is worried that people will think he doesn't wash himself and that the redness means he is having an allergic reaction to his essential Parkinson's medication.
expectations: He hopes to walk away with a prescription-strength medicated shampoo and an easy-to-apply cream that will calm the redness without requiring hard scrubbing.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Seborrheic Dermatitis (severe facial and scalp) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Seborrheic Dermatitis (severe facial and scalp) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management of Seborrheic Dermatitis combines antifungal shampoos and low-potency topical corticosteroids, with closer follow-up in patients whose disease is more severe due to an underlying neurologic condition like Parkinson's.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: greasy, yellowish scales and redness on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest

Key HPI features: 45M with Parkinson disease presenting with chronic pruritic erythematous plaques covered by greasy yellow scales on nasolabial folds and dandruff responding to 2% Ketoconazole shampoo and low-potency hydrocortisone cream.
Objective/Exam findings: Erythematous plaques with greasy, yellowish scale on the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest; no silvery plaques or nail pitting to suggest psoriasis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Seborrheic Dermatitis (severe facial and scalp).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Psoriasis (thicker, more silvery scale) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden, severe, or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis, especially with an underlying neurologic disease like Parkinson's — reflects more severe disease requiring closer follow-up.
management_principles: Initiate 2% ketoconazole shampoo for scalp and facial involvement, applied as a wash-off treatment several times weekly.
Add low-potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone) for inflamed, erythematous areas during flares.
Recognize that Parkinson disease is associated with more severe, treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis and may need closer follow-up.
Refer to dermatology if the disease fails to respond to first-line antifungal and anti-inflammatory therapy.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A chronic inflammatory reaction to Malassezia yeast causing greasy, yellowish scaling on the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds — notably more severe in patients with Parkinson's disease.
red_flags: Sudden, severe, or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis, especially with an underlying neurologic disease like Parkinson's — reflects more severe disease requiring closer follow-up
Signs of secondary bacterial or fungal superinfection (oozing, pain, spreading redness, fever)

must_ask.say: Is the scale greasy and yellowish?
Where is it — your scalp, eyebrows, and around your nose?
Does stress or weather seem to make it worse?

history.answer: I came in because I have these red, itchy patches with greasy yellow flakes on my face, scalp, and chest that won't go away.
It started about six months ago as severe dandruff on my scalp, and then it gradually spread to my eyebrows, the sides of my nose, and my chest.
The red patches and flakes are on my scalp, through both eyebrows, along the folds next to my nose, and over the middle of my chest.
They look like red patches covered in thick, yellowish, oily flakes. There are no fluid-filled blisters or crusted sores.
It itches quite a bit, especially on my scalp and around my eyebrows, but it doesn't sting or hurt.
No, the patches are constantly there and don't come and go or vanish in a few hours like hives would.
I had mild dandruff in the past, but it was never this extensive or red until the past several months.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, body aches, or unusual fatigue.
No, my mouth, lips, eyes, and genital area are completely normal with no blisters, sores, or ulcers.
No, my skin is not peeling off in sheets, and I do not have any dark purple spots or bruises that don't fade when pressed.
No, I have had no swelling of my lips or tongue, no throat tightness, no wheezing, and no trouble breathing.
No, I haven't started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, gout pills, or over-the-counter painkillers recently.
No, I haven't used any new soaps, lotions, colognes, laundry detergents, or metal jewelry, and I haven't handled strange plants.
It tends to flare up and get more itchy when I am stressed, tired, or during cold, dry weather.
No, neither my wife nor anyone I spend time with has any rash or itching.
No, I haven't had any bug bites, haven't been hiking in the woods, and haven't traveled or used public saunas.
No, I have never had asthma, allergic rhinitis, or childhood eczema.
No, my joints don't ache or swell, and my fingernails have no dents, pits, or lifting.
My doctor prescribed a two percent ketoconazole shampoo and a mild hydrocortisone cream, and they help reduce the flaking and redness when I use them regularly.
I have been with my wife for fifteen years in a monogamous relationship, and I have never had any genital ulcers, sores, or discharges.
I was diagnosed with Parkinson disease about three years ago, which causes some stiffness and a resting tremor in my hands.
Other than Parkinson disease, I have no chronic medical conditions like diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take my prescribed Parkinson disease medications, and for my skin, I use the ketoconazole shampoo twice a week and low-potency hydrocortisone cream as needed.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I rarely drink, maybe one glass of beer on a special occasion, but nothing on a regular basis.
I work as an administrative office worker and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father had Parkinson disease later in life, but there is no family history of psoriasis, eczema, or other chronic skin conditions.

I thought it was just really bad dandruff and oily buildup because my shaky hands make it tough for me to wash my face and hair properly in the shower. I'm worried people look at my flaking face and think I'm dirty, or that this is an allergic reaction to my Parkinson's pills and I'll have to stop taking them.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Comfortable and alert 45-year-old male with noticeable facial erythema and flaking, along with mild facial hypomimia.
Erythematous plaques with greasy, yellowish scales on the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and presternal chest; blanching on pressure, without silvery mica-like scales or skin weeping.
Sclerae anicteric, conjunctivae clear without erythema or discharge; eyebrows demonstrate greasy flaking over underlying erythema.
Oral mucosa, tongue, and pharynx are moist and pink without mucosal erosions, ulcerations, or blisters.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical, submandibular, or occipital lymphadenopathy.
No peripheral joint swelling, warmth, or tenderness; fingernails and toenails are intact with no pitting, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis.
Mild resting tremor observed in the right hand with mild bilateral upper-extremity rigidity, consistent with documented Parkinson disease.
